Desmopressin was temporarily held for 48 hours, after which it was resumed at a reduced dose of 180 μg/day in consultation with endocrinology, given the concern that the prior dose may have contributed to the degree of water retention. Cisplatin, a well-recognized cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and, paradoxically, of SIADH-like presentations, was considered a potential contributor to the electrolyte derangement, although the temporal relationship and the pre-existing SIADH phenotype made a multifactorial etiology most likely. On physical examination, her blood pressure was 138/86 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, and body mass index was 24.3 kg/m2. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Fasting plasma glucose was 2.8 mmol/L with a concurrent serum insulin level of 186.4 μIU/mL and C-peptide of 12.3 ng/mL, both markedly elevated. A 72-hour fasting test was performed, during which hypoglycemic episodes recurred with Whipple's triad confirmed. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 2.1 × 1.8 cm hypervascular mass in the pancreatic body. Subsequent endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a well-circumscribed lesion consistent with an insulinoma. The patient underwent distal pancreatectomy with splenic preservation. Postoperative fasting glucose normalized, and nocturnal behavioral episodes ceased entirely. Histopathological examination confirmed a well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (insulinoma, grade 1, Ki-67 index <2%). At six-month follow-up, the patient remained euglycemic with no recurrence of nocturnal episodes.

Given the constellation of descending flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and respiratory compromise in the absence of a toxicological explanation, botulism was strongly suspected. The patient was intubated for airway protection and mechanical ventilation. Stool and serum samples were sent for botulinum toxin testing. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and received heptavalent botulinum antitoxin. Over the following days, his respiratory function gradually improved, and he was extubated on day 4. Full neurological recovery was observed over several weeks, and toxin testing confirmed the diagnosis of foodborne botulism.

Hypertonic saline was not required; instead, oral sodium chloride tablets were initiated and up-titrated, fluid intake was liberalized rather than restricted, and desmopressin was continued at the established dose, given the presumed combined central diabetes insipidus and cerebral salt-wasting physiology. Serum sodium corrected gradually to 132 mEq/L by cycle 1 day 14 and normalized before cycle 2. Hydrocortisone was empirically increased to 50 mg/day during the nadir, then returned to 30 mg/day after clinical improvement, without evidence of adrenal crisis. ICE cycle 2 proceeded at full doses on schedule. During cycle 2, serum sodium declined again to a nadir of 124.6 mEq/L on day 8, with similar urinary sodium and osmolality findings, and again responded to intensified oral sodium supplementation without hypertonic saline or desmopressin adjustment. Cycles 3 and 4 were complicated by milder hyponatremia (nadir 130–133 mEq/L), managed with continued oral sodium chloride and stable endocrine replacement. The patient completed all four planned ICE cycles without dose reduction or treatment delay attributable to sodium disturbances. Restaging imaging after completion of salvage chemotherapy showed no evidence of recurrent disease, and the patient remained in remission

On admission, physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg, a pulse of 78 beats per minute, and a body mass index of 27.8 kg/m2. Neurological examination was unremarkable, with no focal deficits, and the mental status examination was normal. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, electrolytes, and thyroid function, were within normal limits. A fasting plasma glucose of 3.1 mmol/L was noted, with an HbA1c of 5.2%. An overnight polysomnography study confirmed moderate obstructive sleep apnea with an apnea–hypopnea index of 22 events per hour. Prolonged video-electroencephalography captured two typical episodes arising from non-rapid eye movement sleep, without epileptiform discharges. Abdominal ultrasound and pancreatic computed tomography revealed a 1.8 cm mass in the pancreatic tail, suggestive of an insulinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was subsequently performed, and histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. The patient was referred to the Department of Hepatobiliary Surgery for surgical management.

A comprehensive metabolic panel was otherwise unremarkable, and the anion gap was mildly elevated at 14. Given the presentation of acute flaccid paralysis with areflexia, respiratory depression, and altered mental status, suspicion arose for a toxin-mediated syndrome. The patient was intubated for airway protection and started on empirical supportive care. Additional history obtained from the spa staff revealed that he had consumed an herbal tea preparation shortly before being found. A serum sample was subsequently sent for specialized toxicological analysis, which ultimately confirmed the presence of a novel psychoactive substance.
